Flask 6 tries to solve a few of these things by default, but there are other parts you 7 may have to take care of yourself. Many of these solutions are tradeoffs, and 8 will depend on each application's specific needs and threat model. Many hosting 9 platforms may take care of certain types of problems without the need for the 10 Flask application to handle them. 11 12 Resource Use 13 ------------ 14 15 A common category of attacks is "Denial of Service" (DoS or DDoS). This is a 16 very broad category, and different variants target different layers in a 17 deployed application. In general, something is done to increase how much 18 processing time or memory is used to handle each request, to the point where 19 there are not enough resources to handle legitimate requests. 20 21 Flask provides a few configuration options to handle resource use. They can 22 also be set on individual requests to customize only that request. The 23 documentation for each goes into more detail. 24 25 - :data:`MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH` or :attr:`.Request.max_content_length` controls 26 how much data will be read from a request. It is not set by default, 27 although it will still block truly unlimited streams unless the WSGI server 28 indicates support. 29 - :data:`MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE` or :attr:`.Request.max_form_memory_size` 30 controls how large any non-file ``multipart/form-data`` field can be. It is 31 set to 500kB by default. 32 - :data:`MAX_FORM_PARTS` or :attr:`.Request.max_form_parts` controls how many 33 ``multipart/form-data`` fields can be parsed. It is set to 1000 by default. 34 Combined with the default `max_form_memory_size`, this means that a form 35 will occupy at most 500MB of memory. 36 37 Regardless of these settings, you should also review what settings are available 38 from your operating system, container deployment (Docker etc), WSGI server, HTTP 39 server, and hosting platform. They typically have ways to set process resource 40 limits, timeouts, and other checks regardless of how Flask is configured. 41 42 .. _security-xss: 43 44 Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) 45 -------------------------- 46 47 Cross site scripting is the concept of injecting arbitrary HTML (and with 48 it JavaScript) into the context of a website. To remedy this, developers 49 have to properly escape text so that it cannot include arbitrary HTML 50 tags. For more information on that have a look at the Wikipedia article 51 on `Cross-Site Scripting 52 `_. 53 54 Flask configures Jinja to automatically escape all values unless 55 explicitly told otherwise. This should rule out all XSS problems caused 56 in templates, but there are still other places where you have to be 57 careful: 58 59 - generating HTML without the help of Jinja 60 - calling :class:`~markupsafe.Markup` on data submitted by users 61 - sending out HTML from uploaded files, never do that, use the 62 ``Content-Disposition: attachment`` header to prevent that problem. 63 - sending out textfiles from uploaded files. Some browsers are using 64 content-type guessing based on the first few bytes so users could 65 trick a browser to execute HTML. 66 67 Another thing that is very important are unquoted attributes. While 68 Jinja can protect you from XSS issues by escaping HTML, there is one 69 thing it cannot protect you from: XSS by attribute injection. To counter 70 this possible attack vector, be sure to always quote your attributes with 71 either double or single quotes when using Jinja expressions in them: 72 73 .. sourcecode:: html+jinja 74 75 76 77 Why is this necessary? Because if you would not be doing that, an 78 attacker could easily inject custom JavaScript handlers. For example an 79 attacker could inject this piece of HTML+JavaScript: 80 81 .. sourcecode:: html 82 83 onmouseover=alert(document.cookie) 84 85 When the user would then move with the mouse over the input, the cookie 86 would be presented to the user in an alert window. But instead of showing 87 the cookie to the user, a good attacker might also execute any other 88 JavaScript code. In combination with CSS injections the attacker might 89 even make the element fill out the entire page so that the user would 90 just have to have the mouse anywhere on the page to trigger the attack. 91 92 There is one class of XSS issues that Jinja's escaping does not protect 93 against. The ``a`` tag's ``href`` attribute can contain a `javascript:` URI, 94 which the browser will execute when clicked if not secured properly. 95 96 .. sourcecode:: html 97 98 click here 99 click here 100
